## API Design: REST, GraphQL, and gRPC

> **Core Concept:** **REST**, **GraphQL**, and **gRPC** are not competing on quality, they're built for different shapes of problem: resources you fetch and mutate, flexible queries across a graph of data, and fast typed calls between internal services. Picking one is really picking which caller you're optimizing for.

### Why It Matters
- A team defaults to REST for everything because it's what they know, then discovers their mobile app makes six round trips to assemble one screen because no single REST endpoint returns exactly what the screen needs.
- Another team wires two internal microservices together with hand-rolled JSON over HTTP, then spends real engineering time on serialization bugs and slow parsing that a typed, binary protocol would have avoided from day one.
- Without a clear model of what each API style is actually for, engineers argue about which one is 'better' in the abstract, when the real question is always: who is calling this, over what network, and how often does the shape of the request change.

### Intuitive Analogy
Think of ordering food three different ways. REST is a fixed menu: you pick
item number 7, and you get exactly what's on the card for item 7, no more,
no less, if you want something different you order another item. GraphQL is
a buffet where you build your own plate, naming precisely which sides and
how much of each you want in one trip, at the cost of the kitchen having to
support arbitrary combinations. gRPC is calling the chef directly on a
private phone line with a script you both already agree on word for word,
extremely fast and precise, but only useful between people who share that
script, not something you hand to a random customer off the street.


### Key Engineering Principles
- REST models a system as **resources**, nouns like /users/42 or /orders/17, and uses HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to act on them. The URL structure and status codes carry meaning, which makes REST easy to cache, easy to reason about, and understood by essentially every HTTP client and tool that exists.
- REST's core weakness is ==fixed response shapes==: a single endpoint returns a fixed set of fields, so a client that needs data from three resources either makes three requests or the backend grows a special-purpose endpoint just for that one screen, and that pattern repeats until the API is full of one-off endpoints.
- GraphQL exposes a single endpoint backed by a schema describing every type and relationship in the data graph, and the client sends a query naming exactly the fields it wants, nested across relationships, in one round trip. This kills both **over-fetching** (getting fields you don't need) and **under-fetching** (needing a second request to get related data).
- GraphQL moves real complexity to the server: resolving a deeply nested query can silently trigger many expensive database calls (the ==N+1 problem==) unless the server batches them deliberately, and a naive GraphQL server can be trivially asked for a query so large it becomes a denial-of-service vector, which means query cost analysis and depth limiting aren't optional extras.
- gRPC uses **Protocol Buffers**, a compact binary format with a strict schema, and HTTP/2 as transport, to call a remote function almost as if it were local: client.getUser(id) instead of assembling a URL and parsing JSON text. Binary encoding and HTTP/2 multiplexing make it substantially faster and lower-bandwidth than JSON-over-HTTP for high-volume service-to-service traffic.
- gRPC's strict schema (the .proto file) is enforced at compile time on both client and server, catching type mismatches before deployment instead of at runtime like a loosely typed JSON API would. The cost is that gRPC is much less friendly to a browser calling it directly and far less human-readable when you're debugging with a plain text tool.
- REST fits public and partner-facing APIs where wide compatibility, cacheability, and simplicity matter more than squeezing out the last bit of performance, think a payments API or a public product catalog API that many unrelated clients consume.
- GraphQL fits products with many different client shapes pulling from the same underlying graph of data, like a mobile app and a web app that need different slices of the same user/post/comment graph, and where the frontend team wants to move fast without waiting on backend endpoint changes.
- gRPC fits internal service-to-service calls inside one organization's infrastructure, where both ends are services you control, the schema evolves together, and call volume and latency actually matter, not calls made by an arbitrary third-party developer.

## Caching Strategies & Cache Invalidation

> **Core Concept:** A **cache** only helps if it's usually right and cheap to check, and every caching strategy is really a different answer to one question: when the underlying data changes, how does the cache find out, and what does a reader see in the meantime.

### Why It Matters
- Databases are slow relative to memory, and the same data (a user's profile, a product page, a popular post) often gets read far more often than it changes, recomputing or refetching it from scratch on every single read wastes capacity that a cache could save entirely.
- The moment you add a cache, you've created a second copy of the truth, and now you have to decide what happens when the original changes: does the cached copy update immediately, eventually, or does it just quietly go stale and serve wrong data until something notices.
- Phil Karlton's famous line, 'there are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things,' is not a joke about caching being finicky, it's a real acknowledgment that keeping a cache correct under concurrent reads and writes is a genuinely hard distributed systems problem, not an afterthought.

### Intuitive Analogy
A cache is like keeping a printed cheat sheet of your bank balance instead
of calling the bank every time you want to check it. It's fast, you glance
at the paper instead of waiting on hold. But the moment money moves in or
out of the actual account, that paper is wrong until you update it. Do you
update the paper the instant a transaction happens (write-through), let it
happen in the background a moment later (write-back), or just throw the
paper away after an hour and force a fresh call next time you need it
(TTL)? Each choice trades a bit of speed for a bit of risk of looking at
stale numbers.


### Key Engineering Principles
- **Cache-aside** (lazy loading) is the most common pattern: the application checks the cache first, on a miss it reads from the database, then writes the result into the cache for next time. Reads are fast after the first miss, but the cache and database can drift out of sync if the underlying data changes without going through this same path.
- **Write-through** means every write goes to the cache and the database together, synchronously, before the write is considered done. This keeps the cache always consistent with the database, at the cost of every write now paying the latency of two systems instead of one.
- **Write-back** (write-behind) means a write goes to the cache immediately and is considered done, then gets flushed to the database asynchronously later. This makes writes fast, but ==risks data loss== if the cache fails before the flush happens, and needs careful design to avoid it.
- **TTL** (time to live) is the simplest invalidation strategy: every cached entry expires automatically after a set duration, forcing a fresh read from the source of truth. It doesn't require any explicit invalidation logic, but it means the cache can serve ==stale data== for up to the full TTL window, and picking that window is itself a trade-off between staleness and load on the database.
- Explicit invalidation means the application actively deletes or updates a cache entry the moment the underlying data changes, e.g. a user edits their profile, and that write path also deletes the cached profile so the next read is forced to refetch. This gives tighter consistency than TTL alone but requires the application to correctly find and invalidate every cache entry that could be affected by a given write, which gets hard fast as relationships between cached data grow.
- **Cache stampede** (or thundering herd) happens when a popular cached entry expires and a burst of concurrent requests all miss the cache at the same instant, all hammering the database simultaneously trying to refill it. Mitigations include locking so only one request refills while others wait, or staggering TTLs so not everything expires at the same second.
- Eviction policy decides what gets removed when the cache is full, not just when data goes stale. LRU (least recently used) is the most common default, evicting whatever hasn't been accessed in the longest time, on the assumption that recently used data is likely to be used again soon.
- Cache placement matters: a cache can live in the browser (HTTP caching headers), at the CDN edge, in front of an application server (like Redis or Memcached), or even inside a single process's memory. Each layer trades how close (and therefore fast) it is against how much it can hold and how many different clients can share it.
- Choosing what to cache matters as much as how: caching data that's read far more often than it's written, and that can tolerate at least some staleness, gives the best return. Caching data that changes on nearly every read, or where staleness is unacceptable (like real-time account balances), often isn't worth the complexity a cache adds.

## Consistency Models & the CAP Theorem

> **Core Concept:** The **CAP theorem** isn't a menu you pick freely from, network partitions will happen whether you plan for them or not, so the real choice every distributed system makes is what happens during one: keep answering and risk being wrong, or refuse to answer until you can be sure.

### Why It Matters
- The instant a system spans more than one machine connected by a network, that network can fail, a link can drop, a data center can lose connectivity, and the system has to decide what to do in that moment, there's no version of a distributed system that avoids this decision entirely.
- 'Consistency' sounds like a single obvious good thing to want, but there are graded levels of it (strong, eventual, and points between), and the strongest form is often directly in tension with staying available or staying fast, so treating consistency as free or all-or-nothing leads to designs that quietly promise more than they can deliver.
- CAP is one of the most frequently misquoted ideas in system design, misunderstanding what 'partition tolerance' actually means (it's not optional in a real distributed system) leads to wrong conclusions like 'we chose CA', which isn't a real option once a network partition is possible at all.

### Intuitive Analogy
Picture two people running the same small store in two different towns,
sharing one inventory count, connected by a phone line to stay in sync.
As long as the phone line works, easy, they call before every sale to
confirm current stock. Now the phone line goes dead. Each of them has a
choice: stop selling that item until the line's back (consistent, but the
store in each town is now unavailable for that item), or keep selling
based on the last number they had (available, but now both towns might
sell the last unit and one customer gets disappointed later). The phone
line going dead is the partition. What each store does during the outage
is the whole CAP theorem in one story.


### Key Engineering Principles
- The CAP theorem states that a distributed data system can only guarantee two of three properties at once: **Consistency** (every read sees the most recent write, or an error), **Availability** (every request gets a non-error response), and **Partition tolerance** (the system keeps working even when network messages between nodes are lost or delayed).
- Partition tolerance is ==not actually optional== in practice: in any real distributed system, network partitions will happen eventually, a cable gets cut, a data center loses connectivity, a router misbehaves. So the real, live trade-off during an actual partition is between consistency and availability, CP or AP, not a free choice among all three.
- A **CP** system, when a partition happens, chooses consistency: it will refuse to serve a request (or serve an error) rather than risk returning stale or conflicting data. This is the right call for data where being wrong is worse than being unavailable, like a financial ledger.
- An **AP** system, when a partition happens, chooses availability: it keeps answering requests using whatever local data it has, even if that data might be out of sync with the other side of the partition, and reconciles the difference later. This is the right call when staying responsive matters more than momentary staleness, like a social media like counter.
- **Strong consistency** means every read returns the most recent write, as if there were only one copy of the data, no matter which node answers. It's the easiest model to reason about but the hardest to provide cheaply across distant, replicated nodes.
- **Eventual consistency** means that if no new writes happen, all replicas will converge to the same value given enough time, but a read right after a write might return an old value on some replica. This is a much weaker guarantee, but it's often exactly enough for the actual use case, and it's dramatically cheaper to provide at scale.
- There's a real spectrum between the two extremes: read-your-writes consistency (a user always sees their own recent writes, even if others might not yet), causal consistency (operations that are causally related are seen in the same order by everyone, unrelated ones can be seen in different orders), and others. Real systems often pick a specific point on this spectrum rather than the two textbook extremes.
- CAP is specifically about behavior during a partition, it says nothing about normal operation, when the network is healthy, most systems can and do offer both strong consistency and high availability simultaneously. The trade-off only bites during the partition itself, which is exactly why it's easy to under-design for, it works fine until the one day it doesn't.
- PACELC is a useful extension: even without a Partition, there's still a trade-off between Latency and Consistency (the 'ELC' part), because keeping replicas strongly consistent requires coordination that costs time. So the consistency-versus-something trade-off isn't only a partition-time concern, it shows up during normal operation too, just as a latency cost instead of an availability one.

lesson.content:
## Content Delivery Networks (CDNs)

> **Core Concept:** A **CDN** pushes copies of content geographically close to the people requesting it, and it works enormously well for content that's the same for everyone, and barely helps at all for content that's different for every single request.

### Why It Matters
- A single origin server, no matter how powerful, is physically far from most of its users, and the speed of light itself puts a floor on how fast a round trip to a distant server can be, no amount of server tuning fixes that distance.
- A popular video or a viral image can generate an enormous number of near-identical requests for the exact same bytes, and serving every one of them from one origin wastes bandwidth and compute on redundant work the origin already did once.
- A single point of origin is also a single point of failure and a single bottleneck under a traffic spike, a launch, a live event, or a DDoS attack aimed at that one server can take down every user's experience at once.

### Intuitive Analogy
A CDN is like a chain of copy shops instead of one printing press in a
single city. If everyone in the country wants the same flyer, it's far
faster and cheaper to print copies at a shop in every city than to have
every single person mail a request to the one press and wait for a copy to
ship back. But if the flyer needs your name individually printed on it,
that trick stops helping, the shop down the street can't print something
it doesn't have a copy of yet, and now every request really does need to
go back to the one press that knows your name.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A CDN is a distributed network of **edge servers** (points of presence, or PoPs) located in many geographic regions, each holding cached copies of content close to the users in that region, so a request can be served from a nearby edge node instead of crossing the globe to the origin.
- **Origin pull** (lazy caching): the CDN doesn't have the content until the first request for it arrives at an edge node, that first request is forwarded to the origin, the response is cached at the edge, and every subsequent request in that region is served from the cache until it expires. This needs no upfront setup but means the very first user in a region pays the full origin latency.
- **Origin push** (pre-loading): the origin proactively uploads content to CDN edge nodes ahead of any request, guaranteeing every user gets a fast cached response from the first request. This suits content you know in advance will be popular everywhere, like a scheduled major release, at the cost of pushing data to regions that may never actually request it.
- Static assets (images, CSS, JavaScript bundles, downloadable files) are the CDN's best case: the exact same bytes are correct for every single user, so one cached copy at an edge node can serve unlimited requests until the content itself changes, giving a near-perfect cache hit rate.

## Client-Server Architecture & the Request Lifecycle

> **Core Concept:** Every web request you've ever made is a chain of **translations and handshakes**, name to address, address to connection, connection to encrypted channel, before a single byte of your actual data moves, and each link in that chain is a place a system design can add ==latency or fail==.

### Why It Matters
- Typing a URL and seeing a page feels instant and singular, but it's actually a sequence of separate network round trips to separate systems (DNS servers, routers, the destination server), each with its own latency, and treating it as one atomic step hides where a real system actually spends its time.
- Without understanding the request lifecycle, it's easy to misplace blame for slowness, e.g. optimizing server code when the real cost is a slow DNS lookup or an unnecessary extra TLS handshake, or to design a system that repeats expensive steps (like re-resolving DNS or re-negotiating TLS) that could have been reused.
- System design interviews frequently probe this directly ('walk me through what happens when a user hits your API'), and a shaky answer here reads as a gap in fundamentals no matter how good the higher-level architecture is.

### Intuitive Analogy
Getting a web page loaded is like ordering food through a chain of
intermediaries in an old-fashioned office building with no directory.
First you ask the front desk which floor the company you want is on (DNS).
Then you walk to that floor and knock, and someone has to confirm you're
allowed in and agree on a shared language before you can talk business
(the TCP and TLS handshakes). Only after all of that do you actually hand
over your order and get a response (the HTTP request and response). Every
one of those steps takes real time, and if you have to repeat the whole
walk for every single question, you're wasting most of your visit on
logistics instead of getting an answer.


### Key Engineering Principles
- DNS resolution turns a human-readable domain name into an IP address. The browser checks its own cache, then the OS cache, then asks a DNS resolver, which walks a hierarchy (root servers, then top-level domain servers, then the domain's authoritative name server) until it gets an answer, which is then cached according to a TTL so the whole walk doesn't repeat on every request.
- Once the client has an IP address, it opens a TCP connection to the server via a three-way handshake: SYN (client says hello and proposes a starting sequence number), SYN-ACK (server acknowledges and proposes its own), ACK (client confirms). This establishes a reliable, ordered, two-way byte stream before any application data moves.
- For HTTPS, a TLS handshake follows on top of the TCP connection: client and server agree on a cipher suite, the server proves its identity with a certificate signed by a trusted certificate authority, and both sides derive a shared symmetric key used to encrypt everything that follows. This adds one or two extra round trips beyond plain TCP.
- Only after DNS, TCP, and TLS are done does the actual HTTP request go out: a method (GET, POST, etc.), a path, headers (like cookies, content type, authorization tokens), and optionally a body. The server processes it and returns a status code, response headers, and a body.
- **Connection reuse** matters enormously at scale: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive and HTTP/2 multiplexing let a client reuse one already-established (and already TLS-negotiated) TCP connection for many requests, avoiding the handshake cost on every single one. This is why an app that hammers a server with many short-lived connections is often ==slower== than one that reuses a few long-lived ones.
- Latency in this chain comes from physical distance (light itself takes time to travel, which is why CDNs and regional servers exist) and from round trips (each handshake step is a full round trip, so a connection requiring DNS plus TCP plus TLS before the first useful byte can easily cost several times the latency of the actual request).
- The client isn't just a browser. A mobile app, another backend service, or a script calling an API is also 'the client' in this model, and the same lifecycle (resolve a name, open a connection, secure it, exchange data) applies whether the caller is a human with a browser or a server calling another server.
- **Stateless HTTP** means the server, by default, doesn't remember anything about a client between separate requests, each request must carry everything needed to handle it (auth tokens, session identifiers, etc.). This statelessness is a deliberate design choice that trades built-in memory for the ability to route any request to any server, which becomes important the moment a system needs more than one server.
- Persistent connections and connection pooling exist on the server side too: a backend server maintaining a database connection often keeps a pool of already-open connections rather than opening and tearing one down per query, for exactly the same reason clients keep TCP connections alive, opening a connection is expensive relative to using an existing one.

lesson.content:
## Consistent Hashing

> **Core Concept:** **Consistent hashing** exists so that adding or removing one server only reshuffles a small slice of your data, instead of almost all of it.

### Why It Matters
- The obvious way to spread keys across N servers is `hash(key) % N`, but the moment N changes, because a server was added or died, ==nearly every key maps to a different server== than before.
- Remapping nearly every key means nearly every cache or shard is suddenly a miss or in the wrong place at once, exactly when your system is already stressed from a capacity change.
- You need a way to add or remove a server that only affects the small share of data that server was actually responsible for, leaving everyone else's mapping untouched.

### Intuitive Analogy
Picture a big circular clock face with no numbers, just a ring. You write
every server's name at some point around the ring, and you write every
piece of data's name at some point around the ring too, using the same
method (a hash) for both. Each piece of data belongs to the first server
found going clockwise from its spot. Now if you remove one server, only
the data that was walking clockwise straight into that server needs a new
home, everyone else's clockwise walk is completely unaffected because
their neighbors on the ring never moved.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Plain modulo hashing (`hash(key) % N`) ties every key's destination to the total server count N. Changing N from 4 to 5 doesn't just move the keys that should move, it scrambles the mapping for the vast majority of keys, because the modulo operation depends on the exact count.
- Consistent hashing fixes this by mapping both servers and keys onto the same fixed, circular **hash ring** (commonly visualized as a ring from 0 to 2^32-1), independent of how many servers currently exist.
- A key is assigned to the first server encountered walking clockwise around the ring from the key's own position. This is the entire lookup algorithm: hash the key, walk clockwise, stop at the first server.
- Adding a new server only steals the keys that fall between its new ring position and the previous server clockwise from it, everything else on the ring keeps its existing neighbor and is completely unaffected. Removing a server only affects the keys that were pointing to it, which simply fall through to the next server clockwise.
- With only a few real server points on the ring, load can still be very uneven, one server might end up owning a huge arc of the ring just by the luck of where its hash landed, while another owns a tiny sliver.
- **Virtual nodes** solve the uneven-distribution problem: instead of placing each physical server once on the ring, you place it many times (say, 100-200 virtual points), each independently hashed. A server's total share of the ring becomes the sum of many small, scattered slices instead of one big lucky or unlucky arc, which averages out to roughly even.
- Virtual nodes also make failures gentler in practice: when one physical server dies, its 150 virtual points were scattered across many spots on the ring, so its lost traffic gets spread across many surviving servers instead of dumping entirely onto whichever single server happened to be clockwise-adjacent.
- Consistent hashing is what makes distributed caches, sharded databases, and peer-to-peer systems tolerate scaling events gracefully. Without it, every capacity change would come with a mass data-movement event large enough to be an outage on its own.

lesson.content:
## Database Indexing & Query Performance

> **Core Concept:** An **index** is a separate, sorted structure built purely to make reads fast, and every index you add makes writes a little slower and storage a little bigger, so indexing is always a trade, not a free upgrade.

### Why It Matters
- Without an index, finding a row that matches a condition means scanning every row in the table, a **full table scan**, which gets slower in direct proportion to how much data has accumulated.
- You can't index everything for free: every index has to be updated on every insert, update, and delete of the column it covers, so more indexes means ==slower writes== and more disk space.
- Even with the right index in place, a query can accidentally fail to use it, functions applied to a column, mismatched types, or filtering on the wrong side of a composite index can all ==silently force a full scan== anyway.

### Intuitive Analogy
A database table without an index is like a phone book with every entry
in the order people happened to sign up, not alphabetical. Finding one
person means reading every page. An index is the alphabetized version, a
separate, sorted list of names that each point back to a full entry. Building
and keeping that alphabetized list current takes extra work every time
someone joins or leaves, but it turns "read every page" into "flip to
roughly the right spot," which is the entire point.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Most relational database indexes are **B-trees**, a balanced tree structure where every leaf is the same distance from the root, and each node holds a range of sorted keys pointing either to more nodes or to the actual rows. This keeps lookups, range scans, and insertions all **logarithmic** in the number of rows instead of linear.
- A B-tree stays fast because it stays balanced: unlike a plain binary search tree, which can degrade into a slow, lopsided chain under unlucky insert order, a B-tree rebalances itself by splitting full nodes, guaranteeing consistent lookup depth no matter how the data arrived.
- The trade an index makes is explicit: reads get faster because the database can jump almost straight to the matching rows instead of scanning all of them, but every write now also has to update the index's sorted structure, and the index itself takes real **disk space** on top of the table.
- A **composite index** covers multiple columns together, in a specific order, like (last_name, first_name). It can efficiently serve queries that filter on the leftmost columns of that order, but a query that only filters on first_name, skipping last_name, generally can't use it, because the index is sorted by last_name first.
- This **leftmost-prefix rule** is the single most common source of 'why isn't my index being used' confusion: an index on (a, b, c) helps queries filtering on a, or a and b, or a and b and c, but does not help a query that filters on b or c alone.
- An index doesn't help, and the query planner will often skip it, when the query returns a large fraction of the table anyway (a full scan can beat index lookups plus row fetches once you're reading most of the table), when a function or type conversion is applied to the indexed column, or when the column has very ==low cardinality==, like a boolean, where the index barely narrows anything down.
- The **query planner** (in Postgres, MySQL, etc) decides at execution time whether to use an available index at all, based on estimated row counts and statistics about the data's distribution, not just whether an index technically exists. ==Stale statistics== are a real, common cause of a good index suddenly being ignored.
- **Covering indexes** include every column a query needs directly in the index itself, letting the database answer the query from the index alone without a second lookup back to the full row (called avoiding a 'table lookup' or 'bookmark lookup'), which is a meaningful speedup for read-heavy hot paths.
- Write-heavy tables with many indexes pay a real, compounding cost: a single insert might need to update five separate B-trees instead of one, which is why indexing strategy for an **OLTP** system (many small writes) looks very different from an analytics table (few writes, many large reads).

## Distributed Caching Deep Dive

> **Core Concept:** A **cache** is a bet that the same data will be asked for again soon, and every hard caching problem, stampedes, hot keys, eviction, is really just a case where that bet briefly stops paying off.

### Why It Matters
- Reading the same popular data from a database over and over wastes work the database already did once, and at scale that repeated work becomes the thing that falls over first.
- A cache can't hold everything, memory is smaller and pricier than disk, so something has to decide what gets kicked out when it fills up, and a bad **eviction** decision there quietly makes the cache useless.
- Caches introduce their own failure modes that a plain database doesn't have: a popular entry expiring at the wrong moment can send a wall of traffic at the database all at once, that's a ==cache stampede==, and a single overloaded key can bring down one cache node while the rest of the cluster sits idle, that's a ==hot key==.

### Intuitive Analogy
Think of a cache like the small tray of pre-made sandwiches a busy deli
keeps at the front counter, instead of making every sandwich to order from
the back kitchen. It only works because a handful of sandwiches get ordered
constantly, so keeping a few pre-made saves everyone time. But the tray is
small, so the deli has to guess which sandwiches to keep stocked (that's
eviction), and if the one popular tray runs out right as a lunch rush hits,
every single customer suddenly has to wait on the slow kitchen at once
(that's a stampede). And if one sandwich is so popular that a hundred
people want it from the same tray at the same moment, even a fully stocked
tray can't hand them out fast enough (that's a hot key).


### Key Engineering Principles
- Redis and Memcached solve the same core problem, fast in-memory key-value lookups, but differ in what they offer beyond that. Memcached is a pure, multithreaded key-value cache: no persistence, no data structures beyond byte strings, which makes it simple and extremely fast for the one job it does.
- Redis adds real data structures (lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes), optional persistence to disk, built-in replication, and pub/sub. That makes it more than a cache, teams often use it as a lightweight database or message broker too, but it also means a single Redis instance is doing more work per operation than Memcached.
- **Eviction policy** decides what gets thrown out when the cache is full. **LRU** (least recently used) evicts whatever hasn't been touched in the longest time, cheap to approximate and works well when recent access predicts future access, which is true for most real traffic.
- **LFU** (least frequently used) evicts whatever has been accessed the fewest times overall, which protects steady, high-frequency items from being evicted by a short burst of one-time traffic that LRU would mistake for relevance. Most production caches use an approximate LRU or LFU, not the exact version, because tracking exact recency or frequency for millions of keys is itself expensive.
- A **cache stampede** (also called a thundering herd) happens when a single hot key expires and dozens or thousands of requests that were all being served from cache suddenly miss at once and all hit the database simultaneously, often overloading it hard enough to cause a ==cascading outage==.
- Stampedes are prevented with a few standard tricks: a **lock or mutex** so only one request recomputes the value while others wait for it, probabilistic early expiration where a request has a small, increasing chance of refreshing the value before it actually expires, or serving a slightly stale value while one background request refreshes it (**stale-while-revalidate**).
- A **hot key** problem is different from a stampede: it's when one specific key gets so much traffic that the single cache node responsible for it saturates, even though the cluster as a whole has plenty of spare capacity. Consistent hashing spreads keys across nodes evenly, but it can't split one key's traffic across nodes by itself.
- Hot keys are usually fixed by adding a layer above the distributed cache: a small local, in-process cache on each app server for the very hottest handful of keys, or deliberately splitting one hot key into several copies (key_1, key_2, key_3) and picking one at random on read, trading a little staleness or memory for spreading the load.
- Cache-aside (the app checks the cache, and on a miss reads the database and writes the result back into the cache) is the most common pattern because it's simple and the cache and database can't get permanently out of sync from a cache failure. Write-through and write-back patterns exist too, but they couple the cache more tightly into the write path and add complexity most systems don't need.

## Distributed Consensus Basics

> **Core Concept:** **Consensus** is how a group of machines that don't fully trust each other's timing or health still agree on one true answer, and the whole difficulty comes from never being able to tell the difference between 'that node is slow' and 'that node is dead'.

### Why It Matters
- When data is replicated across several machines for durability, they need to agree on what the current value actually is, but the network between them can delay, drop, or reorder messages at any time.
- If a machine goes silent, you genuinely cannot tell from the outside whether it crashed, is just slow, or is still working fine but the network to it is down, and a consensus system has to make progress anyway.
- Naively letting any node accept writes independently leads to ==split-brain==, two nodes each believing they're in charge and accepting conflicting writes that can never be safely merged back together.

### Intuitive Analogy
Imagine a committee of five people who must agree on one decision, but they
can only pass notes through unreliable couriers who sometimes lose a note
or deliver it late. You can't just wait for all five signatures, because
one committee member might be unreachable for hours, or forever. Instead,
the group agrees in advance that a majority (three of five) signing off is
enough to call it decided, and crucially, any future majority is
guaranteed to overlap with this one by at least one person, so a later
decision can never contradict an earlier one without someone noticing.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Consensus is the problem of getting a set of distributed nodes to agree on a single value or sequence of operations, even when some nodes might be slow, crash, or become unreachable, and the network itself can't be trusted to deliver messages promptly or in order.
- A **quorum** is the minimum number of nodes that must participate in a read or write for it to count as valid, typically a strict majority. Requiring a majority for both reads and writes guarantees that any read quorum and any write quorum must overlap by at least one node, which is what lets a read always see the most recent successful write.
- Quorum-based systems tune this overlap deliberately: with N total replicas, a common setup requires **W + R > N** (write quorum plus read quorum greater than total replicas), guaranteeing overlap. You can shift the balance, fewer required for writes and more for reads, or vice versa, trading write latency against read latency depending on which matters more for your workload.
- **Paxos**, in plain terms, works by having a proposer suggest a value and try to get a majority of nodes to promise to accept it, using two phases (a 'prepare' round to lock out older proposals, then an 'accept' round to actually commit the value) specifically so that even if the process is interrupted or multiple proposers compete, the group can never end up agreeing on two different values for the same decision.
- **Raft** solves the exact same problem as Paxos but was explicitly designed to be easier to understand and implement, by separating the process into clearer, more distinct roles and phases: leader election, then log replication, then safety rules for handling leader crashes, instead of Paxos's more unified but harder-to-reason-about mechanism.
- **Leader election** matters because having one node act as the leader for a period of time massively simplifies agreement, the leader can just decide the order of operations and replicate them, rather than every node needing to negotiate every single decision from scratch. Consensus in Paxos and Raft is largely about safely picking a leader and safely detecting and replacing one that's failed.
- A **term or epoch** number is how these systems handle 'the leader might actually still be alive, just unreachable': every time a new leader is elected, it gets a higher term number, and nodes always defer to the highest term they've seen, so an old leader that comes back online after being replaced can never confuse the group into accepting its now-stale decisions.
- None of this is about perfect certainty, it's about a majority agreeing that is provably enough to prevent contradictory outcomes, even though any individual node's true status (alive, dead, or just slow) is ==fundamentally unknowable== from the outside at any given moment.
- Consensus protocols are expensive relative to a plain, unreplicated write: they require multiple network round trips among a majority of nodes before a write is considered durable, which is why they're used ==selectively== (leader election, critical configuration, coordinating distributed locks) rather than for every single piece of data a system stores.

lesson.content:
## Distributed Unique ID Generation

> **Core Concept:** Once more than one machine can create new rows at the same time, a single **auto-incrementing counter** stops being possible, so distributed systems need an ID scheme that many machines can generate correctly without ever talking to each other.

### Why It Matters
- A classic auto-increment primary key relies on exactly one database deciding the next number, which is fine on a single machine but becomes a bottleneck, and eventually a hard limit, once you shard the database across many machines.
- If you let each shard generate its own auto-increment IDs independently, ==two different shards will both eventually produce the ID '1042'==, and merging or comparing data across shards becomes ambiguous or outright broken.
- IDs often need to be sortable by creation time (for pagination, for debugging, for natural chronological ordering) but also need to be generated by many machines at once without coordination, which are two properties that are hard to get simultaneously.

### Intuitive Analogy
Auto-increment is like a single ticket-dispensing machine at one counter,
it works great because there's exactly one machine deciding what number
comes next. Now imagine ten counters need to hand out tickets at the same
time, with no wire connecting them. If each counter just starts counting
from 1 on its own, you'll get ten different "ticket number 7"s. The fix
used by real distributed ID systems is to stamp every ticket with which
counter issued it and roughly when, so two tickets can never collide even
though the counters never once talked to each other.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A plain auto-increment ID works only because a single database instance serializes every insert through one counter. The moment you shard writes across multiple database instances, that single point of coordination is gone, and nothing stops two shards from generating the same next number independently.
- **UUIDs** (specifically UUID v4, randomly generated) solve the collision problem elegantly: 122 bits of randomness makes a collision astronomically unlikely, and any machine can generate one with zero coordination with any other machine.
- The cost of UUIDs is that they carry ==no useful ordering or meaning==, a v4 UUID generated a second ago and one generated an hour ago look equally random, so they sort essentially randomly, which is bad for database index locality (inserting randomly ordered keys into a B-tree index causes far more page splits and fragmentation than inserting roughly sequential ones).
- **Snowflake-style IDs** (popularized by Twitter's original 'Snowflake' service) take a different approach: pack a millisecond timestamp, a worker/machine ID, and a per-millisecond sequence number into a single 64-bit integer, generated locally by each machine with no coordination needed.
- The timestamp bits mean Snowflake-style IDs are roughly sortable by creation time just by comparing the numbers, since the timestamp occupies the most significant bits, which UUIDs fundamentally cannot offer without a separate created_at column.
- The worker ID bits are what prevent collisions between machines: each ID-generating machine or shard is assigned a distinct worker ID (often from a small fixed range, like 10 bits for 1024 possible workers), guaranteeing that even two IDs generated in the exact same millisecond by different machines are still unique.
- The sequence number bits handle the case of one machine generating many IDs within the same millisecond, it's a small local counter that increments per ID within that millisecond and resets to zero at the next millisecond, giving each machine its own mini auto-increment that only needs to avoid colliding with itself.
- This scheme trades a small amount of setup complexity (something has to hand out unique worker IDs, often via a coordination service like Zookeeper or a config value at deploy time) for IDs that are compact (64 bits fits in a native integer, unlike a 128-bit UUID), roughly time-sortable, and generated with zero per-ID network round trips.
- Choosing between UUID and Snowflake-style is mostly a question of what you need: UUIDs when you want dead-simple, fully decentralized generation and don't care about ordering or storage size; Snowflake-style when you want compact, roughly time-ordered IDs and are willing to manage worker ID assignment.
